- [Substack: Is Private Credit the Next Systemic Crisis? Steve Liesman Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 53](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/is-private-credit-the-next-systemic-858) - 2026-04-06

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Recorded March 31, Steve Liesman and Eisman discuss overlapping oil, tariff, monetary-policy and private-credit risks. Eisman emphasizes U.S. resilience and bank capital while expecting software losses. Liesman challenges simple tariff-forecast grading and introduces hidden layers of leverage. A key qualification is that most private loans already carry floating rates, weakening a blanket refinancing-rate-cliff explanation. Bank of America data support lower-income stress alongside continued aggregate spending growth.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

Primary evidence supports the risk channels; neither a recession nor the exact leveraged-equity exposure is established.

Assessment test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.

Further verification: Recheck the original data and subsequent realized outcomes.

- [Consumer Checkpoint: The madness of March](https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/consumer-checkpoint-april-2026.pdf) (2026-04-10): March spending growth was weaker for lower-income households, whose discretionary growth slowed as gasoline budgets increased. Total spending excluding gas still grew 3.6% year over year; larger tax refunds temporarily cushioned pressure.
- [FSB warns on private-credit vulnerabilities](https://www.fsb.org/2026/05/fsb-warns-on-private-credit-vulnerabilities/) (2026-05-06): Identifies opaque valuations, lower-quality leveraged borrowers, sector concentration, layered leverage and bank/insurer linkages; notes rising PIK and some defaults. Report emphasizes data gaps and does not predict a completed systemic crisis.

## Framework and tools

- Evaluate conditional forecasts against the policy actually implemented.
- Separate gross spending transfers from aggregate GDP losses.
- Distinguish supply constraints from demand and inflation-expectation channels.
- Trace leverage through fund, borrower and investor layers.
- Software survival can coexist with impaired pricing and valuation.
- Use private transaction data alongside representative official statistics.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Oil spending-transfer arithmetic and inventories.
- Inflation-expectation surveys and market measures.
- Bank capital and private-credit exposure.
- Floating-rate resets, interest coverage and maturities.
- Income-stratified Bank of America spending data.

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman hosts Steve Liesman. Liesman provides Fed reporting and several explicitly exploratory risks; Eisman supplies his own software, bank-resilience and policy interpretations.
- Full transcript read in two contiguous parts including multiple advertisement breaks and closing recap.
- Explicit recording date March 31, earlier than April 6 publication.
- Steve Liesman and Steve Eisman are distinct speakers; the guest reports some third-party views without endorsing them.
- Debt/equity and asset/equity leverage ratios are used loosely in dialogue and should not be compared without normalization.
